arabian_hubal.name: Answer petitions by the casting of divining-arrows
arabian_hubal.notes: Seven headless divining-arrows (qidāḥ / azlām) were cast by the sanctuary-keeper before Hubal's image to resolve questions of lineage, marriage, travel, blood-money and the dead; the direction of the drawn arrow gave the god's verdict.

sources.reference: Ibn al-Kalbi, Kitab al-Asnam (The Book of Idols)

arabian_hubal.name: Grant the Quraysh fortune and victory in war
arabian_hubal.notes: Hubal was invoked as the war-tutelary of the Quraysh; at the Battle of Uhud the Meccan leader Abu Sufyan is reported to have exalted Hubal as the giver of their success.

sources.reference: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (the Battle of Uhud, 'Exalt Hubal!')

arabian_imru_al_qais.name: Master the qasida and the imagery of the desert ode
arabian_imru_al_qais.notes: Imru' al-Qais is held in the Arabic tradition to be the originator and supreme exemplar of the qasida form, his Mu'allaqa ('Let us halt and weep') ranking first of the seven Suspended Odes for its erotic, equestrian and storm imagery.

sources.reference: Abu al-Faraj al-Isfahani, Kitab al-Aghani; Arberry, The Seven Odes (1957)

armenian_shamiram.name: Raise cities, palaces and waterworks by command
armenian_shamiram.notes: In Khorenatsi's account Shamiram (Semiramis), enthralled by the land of Van, ordered a great city (Shamiramakert) built on the lake-shore with palaces, baths, gardens and an aqueduct/canal bringing fresh water, employing a multitude of workmen.

sources.reference: Movses Khorenatsi, History of the Armenians 1.16

aymara_inti.name: Warm the earth and give light to the living
aymara_inti.notes: As Tata Inti the Sun gives the warmth and light on which highland agriculture and life depend, his daily return greeted at the June-solstice Willkakuti.

sources.reference: Bernabé Cobo, Historia del Nuevo Mundo (1653)

aymara_tunupa.name: Wander among men teaching law, craft and right worship
aymara_tunupa.notes: Tunupa (Tarapaca) journeys through the Collao as a civilizing preacher, rewarding and punishing the peoples and instituting moral and ritual order before being persecuted and cast adrift on Lake Titicaca; the chroniclers merge him with Viracocha.

sources.reference: Joan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti Yamqui, Relación de antigüedades deste reyno del Pirú (c. 1613)

aztec_centeotl.name: Quicken and ripen the maize through its growth
aztec_centeotl.notes: Centeotl embodies the maize plant from seed-corn through the ripening ear; the young-maize feasts of Huey Tozoztli and Xilonen's rites secured the crop he personified.

sources.reference: Sahagún, Florentine Codex, Book 2

aztec_coyolxauhqui.name: Rouse her brothers to assault Coatepec
aztec_coyolxauhqui.notes: Coyolxauhqui leads her four-hundred brothers, the Centzonhuitznahua, in the attack upon their mother Coatlicue at Coatepec, only to be slain and dismembered by the new-born Huitzilopochtli — the myth re-enacted at the Templo Mayor.

sources.reference: Sahagún, Florentine Codex, Book 3 (the birth of Huitzilopochtli)

aztec_mayahuel.name: Suckle the gods of drink from her four-hundred breasts
aztec_mayahuel.notes: Mayahuel nourishes her offspring the Centzon Totochtin ('Four Hundred Rabbits'), the pulque-gods of intoxication, from her many breasts with the fermented maguey-sap; transformed by Quetzalcoatl into the maguey she yields its sweet sap.

sources.reference: Histoyre du Mechique (Garibay); Codex Magliabechiano

aztec_mictecacihuatl.name: Guard the bones of the dead in Mictlan
aztec_mictecacihuatl.notes: With Mictlantecuhtli she keeps the ancestral bones from which humankind is remade; she presides over the souls of those who die of sickness and over the feasts of the dead.

sources.reference: Sahagún, Florentine Codex, Books 3 and 6

aztec_mictlantecuhtli.name: Yield (and contest) the bones for the making of humankind
aztec_mictlantecuhtli.notes: Quetzalcoatl must descend to Mictlan to win from Mictlantecuhtli the ancestral bones; the death-lord sets traps and tricks to keep them, and from the bones the gods grind the present race of men.

sources.reference: Leyenda de los Soles (1558); Histoyre du Mechique

armenian_tsovinar.name: Drive rain, hail and lightning from the clouds
armenian_tsovinar.notes: In the Armenian water-goddess tradition Tsovinar (Nar) is a fierce storm-power who forces rain and hail from heaven and is the personification of thunder and lightning; folklorists describe her riding through the clouds and creating thunderstorms.

sources.reference: Manuk Abeghian, on Armenian folk belief; Russell, Zoroastrianism in Armenia (1987)

armenian_tsovinar.name: Conceive without man by drinking the sea-spring
armenian_tsovinar.notes: In the Daredevils of Sassoun, Tsovinar drinks a handful and a half from the marine Milk-Fountain (Katnaghbyur) and so conceives, without a human father, the twin heroes Sanasar and Baghdasar.

sources.reference: Sasna Tsřer (Daredevils of Sassoun), Cycle 1

arabian_imru_al_qais.name: The Mu'allaqa (Suspended Ode)
arabian_imru_al_qais.notes: His celebrated qasida 'Qifa nabki' ('Halt, let us weep'), reckoned the first and greatest of the seven Mu'allaqat hung (by tradition) at the Ka'ba.

sources.reference: Arberry, The Seven Odes (1957)

aymara_tunupa.name: The twin staffs of the Staff God
aymara_tunupa.notes: The Tiwanaku 'Staff God' of the Gate of the Sun, identified in colonial tradition with Tunupa/Viracocha, grips a staff in each hand, rays terminating in puma- and condor-heads radiating from his head.

sources.reference: studies of the Tiwanaku Gateway of the Sun and the Front-Face/Staff Deity

aztec_mictlantecuhtli.name: Necklace of human eyeballs
aztec_mictlantecuhtli.notes: The death-lord wears a necklace strung with human eyes and earspools of human bone, his headdress crested with owl-feathers and paper banners.

sources.reference: Codex Borgia, pp. 56-60

aymara_inti.name: Golden rayed sun-disk (face of the Sun)
aymara_inti.notes: The Sun is figured as a disk of gold with rays and flames radiating from a central face; the chief image at Cuzco, the Punchao, showed him as a radiant golden boy.

sources.reference: Bernabé Cobo, Historia del Nuevo Mundo (1653), Bk 13

aztec_mictlantecuhtli.name: Cult of the death-lord in the Tlalxicco shrine
aztec_mictlantecuhtli.cadence: calendrical (Mictlan/death day-signs); month of Tititl associated rites
aztec_mictlantecuhtli.notes: Mictlantecuhtli had a temple called Tlalxicco ('navel of the earth') at Tenochtitlan served by a dedicated priesthood; offerings and incense were made to the lord of the dead, and the dead were dispatched to Mictlan with grave-goods and a guiding dog.

sources.reference: Sahagún, Florentine Codex, Books 2-3 and Book 6 (the funeral rites)

aztec_mictecacihuatl.name: Feasts of the dead in the ninth month
aztec_mictecacihuatl.cadence: annual, the 'great feast of the dead' (Hueymiccailhuitl)
aztec_mictecacihuatl.notes: The Lady of the Dead presided over the festivals of the dead, the lesser and greater 'feasts of the dead' (Miccailhuitontli and Hueymiccailhuitl) in which offerings were made for the departed — practices later folded into the Day of the Dead.

sources.reference: Sahagún, Florentine Codex, Book 2 (the ceremonies of the months)

aztec_coyolxauhqui.name: Re-enactment of Coatepec on the Coyolxauhqui monolith
aztec_coyolxauhqui.cadence: annual, at the feast of Panquetzaliztli
aztec_coyolxauhqui.notes: At the foot of Huitzilopochtli's stair lay the great relief of the dismembered moon-goddess; sacrificial victims cast down the temple steps re-enacted Coyolxauhqui's defeat and fall at Coatepec.

sources.reference: Sahagún, Florentine Codex, Books 2-3
Matos Moctezuma, The Great Temple of the Aztecs (1988)

attributes.name: Red-agate man with a golden hand
attributes.notes: Hubal's image was a man of red agate (cornelian); it reached the Quraysh with the right hand broken off, and they replaced it with a hand of gold. It stood within the Ka'ba over the treasure-pit.

sources.reference: Ibn al-Kalbi, Kitab al-Asnam

attributes.name: The seven divining-arrows
attributes.notes: Seven headless arrows (qidāḥ) stood before the image, drawn by the keeper to deliver the god's verdicts.

sources.reference: Ibn al-Kalbi, Kitab al-Asnam

attributes.name: Black sacred stone at Qudayd
attributes.notes: Manat was venerated as a great black stone (an outcrop) on the sea-road at Qudayd between Mecca and Medina, anointed and circumambulated by the Aws and Khazraj.

sources.reference: Ibn al-Kalbi, Kitab al-Asnam

attributes.name: Goddess of fate and the appointed death
attributes.notes: As the apportioner of destinies and death, Manat (whose name links to maniyya, 'fate/death') was invoked to protect tombs in the Nabataean north and to guarantee oaths.

sources.reference: Nabataean funerary inscriptions invoking Manawat (Hegra/Madā'in Sālih)

attributes.name: Mural (turret) crown
attributes.notes: Especially on coins the Dea Syria wears the crenellated mural crown of the city she protects, marking her as tutelary city-goddess.

sources.reference: coinage of Hierapolis-Bambyce; Lightfoot, Lucian: On the Syrian Goddess (2003)

attributes.name: Scepter and spindle, enthroned between lions
attributes.notes: Lucian describes her seated image holding a scepter in one hand and a spindle in the other, rays about her head and lions at her sides; the fish-tailed Derceto form belongs to Ascalon.

sources.reference: Lucian (attrib.), De Dea Syria §32

sacredPlants.name: Sacred dove-trees of the temple court
sacredPlants.notes: The sanctuary at Hierapolis kept sacred trees thronged with the goddess's inviolable doves, beside the pools of her sacred fish.

sources.reference: Lucian (attrib.), De Dea Syria §§41, 45-47

attributes.name: Forked thunderbolt and mace
attributes.notes: The Syro-Hittite weather-god is figured bearded, striding upon or beside his bull, brandishing a mace and grasping a forked lightning-bolt or sheaf of stylized lightning.

sources.reference: Green, The Storm-God in the Ancient Near East (2003)

attributes.name: Horned crown
attributes.notes: As a high storm-god he wears the horned headdress of divinity in Near Eastern convention.

sources.reference: Green, The Storm-God in the Ancient Near East (2003)

sacredAnimals.name: Chariot and team of the divine charioteer
sacredAnimals.notes: Rakib-El, 'Charioteer of El,' is the dynastic god who drives the divine chariot; on the Bar-Rakib orthostats his royal devotee is shown with the winged solar/lunar disc emblem of the Samalian house, and the god is paired in the inscriptions with the moon-god Baal-Harran.

sources.reference: Bar-Rakib inscriptions and reliefs, Zincirli (KAI 216-218)

attributes.name: Radiant golden face emitting rays and flames
attributes.notes: Inti is shown as a human face of gold from which sun-rays and flames stream; gold itself was held to be the 'sweat of the Sun.'

sources.reference: Bernabé Cobo, Historia del Nuevo Mundo (1653)

sacredAnimals.name: Condor (mallku) of the sky
sacredAnimals.notes: The condor, lord of the upper world (alaxpacha), is the bird associated with the solar/celestial sphere in Aymara cosmology.

sources.reference: Bastien, Mountain of the Condor (1978)

attributes.name: Earth-mother bearing crops, embodied in stone and tree
attributes.notes: Pachamama is imagined as a woman laden with potatoes and coca, present in the soil itself; her shrines are sacred rocks (apachetas) and ancient tree-trunks of the altiplano.

sources.reference: colonial idolatry literature; Bastien, Mountain of the Condor (1978)

sacredPlants.name: Coca leaf
sacredPlants.notes: Coca (the k'intu of three perfect leaves) is the foremost offering laid to and burned for the earth-mother in the challa and despacho rites.

sources.reference: Tschopik, The Aymara of Chucuito (1951)

attributes.name: Many-breasted goddess enthroned on a tortoise amid the maguey
attributes.notes: Mayahuel is depicted seated within or upon a flowering maguey, sometimes on a tortoise, with multiple breasts (linked to her 'four hundred' children) and the crescent yacametzli nose-ornament of the pulque-gods.

sources.reference: Codex Borgia; Codex Laud

sacredPlants.name: Maguey (agave) plant
sacredPlants.notes: The maguey into which she was transformed is her body and emblem; its sap (aguamiel) ferments to the sacred pulque.

sources.reference: Histoyre du Mechique; Codex Magliabechiano

sacredAnimals.name: Owl (tecolotl)
sacredAnimals.notes: The screech-owl is the death-bird and harbinger of Mictlan that attends the death-lord.

sources.reference: Miller & Taube, The Gods and Symbols of Ancient Mexico and the Maya (1993)

sacredAnimals.name: Bat
sacredAnimals.notes: The cave-dwelling bat, associated with the dark underworld passage, belongs to his death-imagery.

sources.reference: Codex Borgia, pp. 56-60

sacredAnimals.name: Spider
sacredAnimals.notes: Spiders, creatures of the dark earth, appear among the death-fauna attending him in the codices.

sources.reference: Codex Borgia, pp. 56-60

sacredAnimals.name: Dog (Itzcuintli)
sacredAnimals.notes: Mictlantecuhtli rules the day-sign Itzcuintli (dog); a dog guides the soul across the river to Mictlan.

sources.reference: Sahagún, Florentine Codex, Books 3 and 6

attributes.name: Skull face, gaping jaw and serpent skirt
attributes.notes: The Lady of the Dead is a skeletal woman, her flesh-stripped face with gaping jaw and bared teeth, wearing a skirt of serpents and with drooping breasts.

sources.reference: Miller & Taube, The Gods and Symbols of Ancient Mexico and the Maya (1993)

attributes.name: Dismembered body within a ring of stars
attributes.notes: The Templo Mayor monolith shows the moon-goddess decapitated and her limbs severed, bound at the joints, encircled by star-symbols — the defeated moon at the foot of the war-god's pyramid.

sources.reference: Matos Moctezuma, The Great Temple of the Aztecs (1988)

attributes.name: Golden bells on the cheeks
attributes.notes: Her name 'Painted-with-Bells' is shown by the golden bells (coyolli) marked on her cheeks.

sources.reference: Miller & Taube, The Gods and Symbols of Ancient Mexico and the Maya (1993)

sacredPlants.name: Maize (cintli)
sacredPlants.notes: The maize plant and its ripening ear are the body and emblem of the maize-god, borne in his headdress.

sources.reference: Sahagún, Florentine Codex, Book 2

attributes.name: Frontal staff-bearing 'Weeping God' with rayed head
attributes.notes: In the Tiwanaku tradition that the chroniclers attach to Tunupa/Viracocha, the deity is the Gate-of-the-Sun 'Staff God': a frontal figure on a stepped platform holding a staff in each hand, rays tipped with puma- and condor-heads radiating from the head, with tear-bands beneath the eyes (the 'crying god').

sources.reference: studies of the Tiwanaku Gateway of the Sun (Staff/Front-Face Deity)

sacredAnimals.name: Puma
sacredAnimals.notes: Puma-heads terminate the divine rays and recur across Tiwanaku staff-god imagery linked to the thunder-and-creator deity.

sources.reference: Tiwanaku iconographic scholarship on the Staff God
